content: In a pooled analysis of four studies, two of the studies included children of all ages, with upper age limits of 10 and 14 years, respectively. The median age of participants in one study was 5 years, while the mean age in the other was 6 years. There was a potential risk of selection bias in one observational study, as villages with high trachoma prevalence received mass drug administration (MDA) of azithromycin, whereas those with low prevalence did not. This study contributed 40% of the weight in the pooled analysis. Data on the number of patients and absolute effects could not be estimated for acute respiratory tract infections and diarrhea because one study (Coles 2011) reported data as episodes per person-years. The WHO guideline on mass drug administration of azithromycin to children under five years of age to promote child survival includes a PRISMA flowchart detailing the article selection process for review. For one review, 13 records were identified through MEDLINE and 9 through Embase, with 16 records remaining after duplicates were removed. Of these, 27 records were screened, 7 were excluded, and 20 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Two articles were excluded with rationale, leaving 18 studies included in the qualitative synthesis. An additional 11 records were identified through other sources. For another review, 10,256 records were identified through database searches (MEDLINE: 2,064; Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials: 761; Embase: 5,647; International Pharmaceutical Abstracts: 152; CINAHL: 433; PubMed: 1,999). After duplicates were removed, 7,450 records remained. Of these, 7,038 were excluded for reasons such as not being the appropriate study type (4,318), not involving children (1,075), not using azithromycin monotherapy (820), lacking safety reports (401), or being duplicates (424). A total of 412 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, with 293 excluded for reasons such as not involving children (99), not using azithromycin monotherapy (89), lacking safety reports (58), or lacking full text (47). Ultimately, 119 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, comprising 77 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 29 cohort studies, 11 case reports, and 2 pharmacokinetic studies. The WHO guideline acknowledges the contributions of numerous experts and organizations in its development. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was co-chaired by Maharaj K. Bhan (Indian Institute of Technology, India) and Robert E. Black (Johns Hopkins University, USA), with Roger Chou (Oregon Health Sciences University, USA) serving as the methodologist. The group included experts in child health, epidemiology, clinical pharmacology, infectious diseases, and bioethics from various institutions worldwide. External peer reviewers also contributed, including specialists in pediatric clinical pharmacology, biostatistics, tropical medicine, and public health. The guideline development process was supported by a grant from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). The recommendations are based on the advice of independent experts who considered the best available evidence, risk-benefit analyses, and other relevant factors. The publication may include recommendations for the use of medicinal products outside their approved labeling, and stakeholders are advised to familiarize themselves with applicable national legal and ethical requirements.
